Results of the laboratory testing completed at Oak Ridge National Laboratory (ORNL) demonstrated that the systems met all requirements of the Challenge. Carrier Corporation has successfully completed this aspect of the Challenge. This CRADA report will briefly describe the Challenge, the test plan created to measure the success of systems provided by Challenge participants, and the results of laboratory testing of the Carrier commercial rooftop systems. 1. STATEMENT OF OBJECTIVES Heating, ventilation, and air-conditioning (HVAC) requires significant energy for commercial businesses in the US. A common method of providing HVAC to commercial buildings is the use of packaged rooftop units that combine the functions of heating, cooling, and dehumidifying in one product that is commonly installed on the building’s roof. The US DOE has challenged HVAC original equipment manufacturers (OEMs) to develop innovative rooftop systems to meet groundbreaking goals for energy efficiency through a range of ambient conditions. Successful development of these systems will allow commercial business and property owners to meet their cost, energy, and reliability needs. Therefore, the objective of this CRADA was to demonstrate that two prototypes developed by Carrier Corporation meet the targets specified by DOE through laboratory testing at Oak Ridge National Laboratory (ORNL). The smaller capacity prototype was a nominal 10-ton capacity, while the larger was a nominal 15-ton capacity. 2. BENEFITS TO THE BUILDING TECHNOLOGY OFFICE’S MISSION This project will supports the mission of the Building Technologies Office (BTO) Commercial Buildings Integration (CBI) Program, to identify and develop technologies that dramatically reduce commercial building energy consumption. The specific CBI initiative, the Commercial Building HVAC Technology Challenge, estimates that high efficiency rooftop units (RTUs) can reduce energy costs by up to 50% compared with conventional RTUs, but fewer than 15% of commercial buildings in the U.S. currently have them. 1 2.1 TECHNICAL SPECIFICATIONS For the unit under test (UUT), the minimum performance requirements were sub-divided into categories of General Requirements, Cooling Performance, Heating Performance, and Controls Verification Procedure (CVP). American National Standards Institute/American Society of Heating, Refrigerating, and Air- Conditioning Engineers (ANSI/ASHRAE) 37-2009.[3] 2.1.1 General Requirements The prototypes submitted for testing were required to meet all applicable federal and state standards, regulations, and laws that govern rooftop HVAC systems. The refrigerants that were used in these systems were to have been approved by the U.S. Environmental Protection Agency (EPA) Significant New Alternatives Policy (SNAP) and they were to comply with the EPA technology transitions program for light commercial HVAC equipment. The prototypes submitted for testing were to be single-zone packaged units with air -cooled direct expansion mechanical heating and cooling systems.
